name: Corned Beef & Cabbage with Potatoes and Carrots
description: The St. Patrick's week centerpiece: a salt-cured brisket slow-braised with cabbage wedges, waxy potatoes, and sweet carrots until everything is fork-tender and perfumed with bay, mustard seed, and black pepper. Serve with whole-grain mustard and a good crusty bread. This is Wednesday's locked dinner — early release day, cold weather (43°F/27°F), and the kind of meal that fills the house with warmth.
why: Wednesday locked. Cold-weather comfort, feeds an 8-year-old easily (potatoes + carrots she loves). Creates leftover corned beef for two more dinners this week — the tacos and the kimchi rice bowls.

name: Corned Beef Tacos with Quick Pickled Onions & Mustard Crema
description: Shredded leftover corned beef gets a second life in warm flour tortillas with tangy quick-pickled red onions, shredded cabbage (also from Wednesday's leftovers), a bright mustard crema, and a squeeze of lime. The salty, beefy filling needs almost no embellishment — the toppings do the work.
why: Creative leftover reuse — zero waste cooking at its best. Taco night is always a win with Elsie. The mustard crema bridges the Irish and Mexican flavor profiles. 15 minutes from fridge to table.

name: Babo Pasta (Homemade Spinach Pasta with Egg Yolks)
description: The family's signature dish: silky fresh pasta made with spinach puree and golden egg yolks, rolled thin and cut by hand. The sauce is almost irrelevant because the pasta itself is the star — buttery, verdant, and impossibly smooth. Toss with brown butter and Parmesan, or a simple garlic-olive oil finish.
why: Non-negotiable family favorite and the Italian requirement. Yes, it appeared in 3 of the last 4 plans — the family wants what they want. Elsie helps roll the pasta. Consider varying the sauce this week (cacio e pepe finish? lemon cream?).

name: Big Dinner Salad — Vegetarian Night
description: A substantial, composed dinner salad built on mixed greens with roasted chickpeas, shaved Parmesan, toasted pepitas, avocado, shredded carrots, pickled beets, soft-boiled eggs, and a punchy lemon-tahini dressing. This is a real dinner, not a side dish — hearty enough to satisfy the whole family while keeping the night plant-forward.
why: Vegetarian night anchor. The chickpeas and eggs provide protein, the beets and avocado make it feel substantial. Every element is Elsie-friendly when separated — she can build her own plate. Mid-March produce works here: sturdy greens, root vegetables, good citrus still in season.

name: Corned Beef Kimchi Fried Rice Bowls
description: Day-old rice gets stir-fried in sesame oil with diced leftover corned beef, chopped aged kimchi, a splash of gochujang, and soy sauce until everything is caramelized and nutty. Crown each bowl with a runny fried egg, sliced scallions, toasted sesame seeds, and a drizzle of sriracha mayo. The salty corned beef and tangy kimchi are a shockingly good pairing.
why: Third act for the corned beef — brilliant leftover arc (Wed → Thu/Fri → later in the week). The kimchi-corned beef combo sounds odd but is genuinely delicious: salty, funky, umami. Elsie gets her fried egg and rice. Fast weeknight dinner.

name: Bangers & Colcannon with Onion Gravy
description: Proper Irish pub comfort: meaty pork sausages browned and nestled into a cloud of colcannon — creamy mashed potatoes folded with sautéed kale, scallions, and butter — all draped in a dark, savory onion gravy. The colcannon can be prepped ahead and reheated, making this a fast-serve dinner for a busy evening.
why: 🍀 St. Patrick's Day! Tuesday is swim lessons 6:00-6:30, so dinner must be FAST. Make the colcannon before swim, brown sausages after — 10 minutes to plate. Cold weather (41°F) demands this kind of warmth. Elsie loves mashed potatoes. Sausages = automatic kid approval.

name: One-Pot Shrimp & Andouille Jambalaya
description: A hearty Louisiana one-pot with smoky andouille sausage, juicy shrimp, the Cajun holy trinity (celery, onion, bell pepper), crushed tomatoes, and long-grain rice simmered until the rice absorbs all that spiced, smoky broth. Shrimp goes in at the very end so it stays plump and tender. Bold, warming, deeply satisfying.
why: From the family 'want to make someday' list! One pot = minimal cleanup. Shrimp + sausage = two new proteins this week. Keep mild for Elsie by reducing cayenne. Saturday evening is ideal — warm day (60°F), Elsie's been at art camp and swimming, everyone's hungry.

name: Lamb Kofta Flatbreads with Tzatziki & Cucumber Salad
description: Warmly spiced ground lamb mixed with parsley, cumin, coriander, and a pinch of cinnamon, shaped into oval logs and grilled or pan-fried until charred outside, juicy inside. Serve on warm pita or naan with cool tzatziki, diced cucumber-tomato salad, and pickled onions. A build-your-own format that lets everyone customize — Elsie assembles her own flatbread.
why: Middle Eastern requirement ✓. Lamb is a new protein not seen in the last 4 weeks. Build-your-own format is an instant win with kids — Elsie gets to play chef. Friday (no school) is perfect: more time to cook and eat together. The spice profile (cumin, coriander) is adjacent to the Cajun seasoning in the jambalaya — similar warmth, completely different cuisine.

name: Shakshuka with Crusty Bread
description: Eggs poached in a vibrant, spiced tomato-pepper sauce with cumin, paprika, and a touch of harissa — scooped up with torn pieces of crusty sourdough. A one-skillet wonder that's vegetarian, deeply comforting, and ready in 25 minutes. Crumble feta on top for richness.
why: Second Middle Eastern option ✓. Vegetarian ✓. Could pair with the 'big salad' night or stand alone. Eggs are the protein Elsie already loves. The tomato-cumin base is adjacent to the jambalaya's tomato-spice base — same warmth, totally different result. No roasted red peppers (Elsie's no-go). Sunday's drizzly, cloudy weather calls for this.

name: Irish Seafood Chowder with Brown Bread
description: A creamy, luxurious chowder loaded with salmon, cod, and shrimp in a silky base of leeks, potatoes, and cream, finished with fresh dill and a squeeze of lemon. Served with thick slices of toasted Irish brown bread. This is coastal Ireland in a bowl — warming, elegant, and surprisingly quick.
why: Another Irish option for St. Patrick's week — different from the corned beef and bangers. Seafood protein adds variety. Creamy + warm for the cold early week. Could work Sunday (56°F, slight rain) or Tuesday as a St. Patrick's Day alternative. Elsie likes salmon.

name: Mujadara (Lentils & Rice with Crispy Onions)
description: A humble but magnificent dish of spiced green or brown lentils cooked with basmati rice, topped with an absurd mountain of deeply caramelized, crispy fried onions. Served with a cooling yogurt sauce and a simple salad. This is peasant food elevated — cheap, nutritious, vegetarian, and the crispy onions make it completely addictive.
why: Third Middle Eastern option ✓. Vegetarian ✓. Adjacent to the kimchi rice bowls (rice + bold topping), but completely different flavor world. The crispy onions are the hook for Elsie — she'll eat anything with crunchy fried onions. Lentils are a protein she hasn't had recently. Budget-friendly anchor in a week with corned beef and shrimp.

name: Baba Ganoush with Warm Pita Chips
description: Smoky roasted eggplant mashed with tahini, lemon juice, garlic, and a drizzle of good olive oil. Served with warm, crisp pita chips brushed with za'atar butter. The smoky-creamy dip is a perfect bridge appetizer between the week's Middle Eastern and Irish flavors — smoke connects to both traditions.
why: Ties the Middle Eastern thread together. Smoky eggplant is a flavor Elsie hasn't encountered much — adventurous but approachable with the pita chips as a safe entry point. Great make-ahead appetizer for the weekend.

name: Irish Cheddar & Herb Soda Bread
description: A quick, no-yeast bread enriched with sharp Irish cheddar, fresh chives, and a touch of butter, with the classic soda bread tang from buttermilk. Bakes in 40 minutes, fills the house with the smell of fresh bread. Slice thick and serve warm with Irish butter. Perfect St. Patrick's week baking project — Elsie can help mix and shape the dough.
why: St. Patrick's week demands soda bread. The cheddar makes it more of a standalone appetizer than plain soda bread. Pairs with the chowder, the corned beef, or just butter. Elsie baking project for Wednesday's early release.

name: Fattoush with Crispy Pita, Sumac & Pomegranate Dressing
description: A composed dinner salad of torn romaine, cucumber, tomatoes, radishes, and fresh herbs (mint, parsley) tumbled with shards of fried pita bread, dressed in a bright sumac-pomegranate molasses vinaigrette. Add chickpeas or grilled halloumi for protein to make it a full dinner.
dressing: Sumac-Pomegranate Vinaigrette: Whisk 3 Tbsp olive oil, 2 Tbsp lemon juice, 1 Tbsp pomegranate molasses, 1 tsp sumac, 1 minced garlic clove, salt and pepper. The sumac adds a citrusy tartness, the pomegranate molasses brings fruity depth.
flavor_rationale: Bridges the week's Middle Eastern thread into salad form. The crispy pita provides textural contrast that keeps kids engaged. Sumac's lemony tang pairs naturally with the lamb kofta or shakshuka — serve alongside either for a complete Middle Eastern dinner.
seasonal_note: Mid-March on the East Coast: hothouse tomatoes are still better than field tomatoes, but good enough for fattoush. Radishes are starting their early spring season — look for Easter Egg radishes at farmers' markets. The herbs (mint, parsley) are transitional — grocery store is fine.
why: The composed dinner-sized salad. Middle Eastern through-line. The crispy pita is the hook for Elsie — it's essentially eating a salad with chips.

name: Spring Greens Salad with Bacon, Poached Egg & Warm Mustard Vinaigrette
description: A Lyonnaise-inspired dinner salad: sturdy frisée and mixed spring greens dressed in a warm bacon vinaigrette made with whole-grain mustard, sherry vinegar, and the rendered bacon fat itself. Topped with a trembling poached egg, crispy lardons, croutons, and shaved Gruyère. When you break the egg, the yolk becomes part of the dressing.
dressing: Warm Mustard-Bacon Vinaigrette: Cook 4 slices diced bacon until crispy, remove. In the rendered fat, sauté 1 minced shallot until soft. Off heat, whisk in 2 Tbsp sherry vinegar, 1 Tbsp whole-grain mustard, 1 tsp Dijon, and 2 Tbsp olive oil. Season with salt and pepper. Pour warm over greens to slightly wilt them.
flavor_rationale: The warm dressing wilts the greens just slightly — perfect for a cold March evening when you want salad but also want warmth. The bacon-mustard-egg trifecta is universally loved. Adjacent to the corned beef's mustard notes — same condiment, totally different context.
seasonal_note: Early spring greens (frisée, arugula, mâche) are starting to appear at East Coast markets but are still delicate. Supplement with heartier supermarket mixed greens. Sherry vinegar's warmth suits the transitional weather better than a bright citrus dressing would.
why: The tossed dinner-sized salad. French bistro vibe for a change of pace from the week's Irish and Middle Eastern focus. Bacon + egg = Elsie-proof.

name: Cucumber-Tomato Salad with Lemon-Za'atar Dressing
description: A simple, clean chopped salad of diced cucumber, cherry tomatoes, red onion, and fresh parsley, dressed in lemon juice, olive oil, and a generous dusting of za'atar. Refreshing, crunchy, and ready in 5 minutes — the perfect cool counterpoint to rich mains like kofta or corned beef.
dressing: Lemon-Za'atar Dressing: Whisk 3 Tbsp extra-virgin olive oil, 2 Tbsp fresh lemon juice, 1 tsp za'atar, pinch of Aleppo pepper (optional), salt to taste. Simple, bright, herbaceous.
flavor_rationale: Za'atar's thyme-sesame-sumac blend echoes the fattoush's sumac notes without repeating it. The simplicity of this salad lets it pair with virtually anything — serve alongside the kofta flatbreads, the kimchi rice bowls, or even the corned beef.
seasonal_note: Persian cucumbers and cherry tomatoes are available year-round from hothouses. In mid-March, the tomatoes won't be peak-season sweet, but the za'atar and lemon compensate beautifully. This salad travels well in a packed lunch for Saturday's events.
why: Side salad #1. Five-minute assembly, no cooking, pairs with everything. Elsie eats cucumbers by the bag.

name: Shaved Fennel & Green Apple Slaw with Cider Vinaigrette
description: Paper-thin shaved fennel and matchstick green apple tossed with celery leaves, toasted walnuts, and a tangy apple cider vinaigrette. Light, crunchy, and palate-cleansing — the anise note from the fennel is subtle enough for kids when balanced by the sweet apple.
dressing: Cider Vinaigrette: Whisk 3 Tbsp olive oil, 1.5 Tbsp apple cider vinegar, 1 tsp Dijon mustard, 1 tsp honey, salt and pepper. The honey rounds out the vinegar's sharpness and bridges to the apple's sweetness.
flavor_rationale: Fennel's mild anise cuts through the richness of the corned beef and sausages — pair this alongside the bangers & colcannon or the corned beef dinner. The apple adds sweetness that kids respond to. Walnuts bring earthy depth that connects to the week's hearty dishes.
seasonal_note: Fennel is in solid mid-season through March on the East Coast — look for firm, white bulbs with bright fronds. Granny Smith apples hold up perfectly this time of year. This slaw actually improves after 30 minutes of sitting, making it ideal for prep-ahead nights.
why: Side salad #2. The textural crunch and clean anise note provide the palate cleanser this rich, meaty week desperately needs. Fennel hasn't appeared in any recent plans.

name: Dry Irish Stout (Guinness Draught)
description: The iconic creamy, dark stout with notes of roasted barley, coffee, and dark chocolate. Despite its appearance, Guinness is actually lighter in body and calories than most craft beers. The nitro-charged pour creates that legendary cascading effect.
why: St. Patrick's week — non-negotiable. Pairs perfectly with the corned beef, the bangers, and the chowder. The roasted bitterness cuts through the richness of all three. Keep a few cans cold for the whole week.

name: Vinho Verde (Quinta da Aveleda)
description: A crisp, slightly effervescent Portuguese white wine with notes of green apple, citrus, and white flowers. Low alcohol (9-11%), high refreshment. The gentle fizz makes it feel festive without being heavy — perfect for transitional March weather that can't decide if it's winter or spring.
key_ingredients: Vinho Verde — look for Quinta da Aveleda or Broadbent labels, widely available, $8-12
why: Pairs beautifully with the seafood chowder, the shakshuka, and the big dinner salad. The slight effervescence lifts rich dishes and cuts through cream. Budget-friendly for a weeknight bottle. The citrus notes echo the lemon-tahini and za'atar dressings throughout the week.

name: Sparkling Mint-Cucumber Lemonade (Mocktail)
description: A refreshing family-friendly mocktail: muddled fresh mint and thin cucumber slices stirred with fresh lemon juice and simple syrup, topped with sparkling water and ice. Garnish with a cucumber ribbon and a sprig of mint. Elsie can help muddle the mint — make it a kitchen activity.
why: The kid-friendly anchor. Elsie loves making drinks. The cucumber-mint profile is a gentle nod to the week's Middle Eastern flavors (think: the tzatziki's cucumber-yogurt, the za'atar salad's brightness). Refreshing for the warmer end-of-week days (59-60°F). Make a big pitcher for Saturday's packed lunch.
